summary.text: The counterexample is \(n=896315812331399\); monotonicity bounds \(z<282\) and leaves only finitely many feasible \((y,z)\), which are exhaustively checked.  For each residual, the identity \(6(\binom W2+\binom X4)+1=Q(X(X-3)/2+W,2W-1)\), with \(Q(a,b)=a^2-ab+b^2\), reduces the problem to an Eisenstein-norm obstruction: factorization either finds a prime \(q\equiv2\pmod3\) to an odd exponent or permits enumeration of all norm representations up to units, none satisfying the parity and square conditions forced by \(W,X\).

full_proof.text:
We disprove the conjecture by exhibiting the positive integer
\[
 n_0=896315812331399
\]
and proving that it has no representation
\[
 n_0=\binom W2+\binom X4+\binom Y6+\binom Z8
 \qquad(W,X,Y,Z>1).
\]
It is enough to consider
\[
 W\ge2,\qquad X\ge3,\qquad Y\ge5,\qquad Z\ge7.                 \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the omitted lower arguments of the fourth-, sixth-, and eighth-order binomial coefficients all give zero and can respectively be replaced by 3, 5, and 7. Thus proving nonexistence under (1) proves nonexistence for all arguments greater than one.

The proof combines an algebraic reduction to the Eisenstein norm with a finite exact-integer calculation. We first give all of the mathematics that makes that calculation exhaustive.

1. The Eisenstein norm and the key identity

Put
\[
 Q(a,b)=a^2-ab+b^2.
\]
This is the norm form in the Eisenstein integers. If multiplication of pairs is defined by
\[
 (c,d)*(a,b)=(ca-db,\;cb+da-db),                              \tag{2}
\]
then direct expansion gives
\[
 Q((c,d)*(a,b))=Q(c,d)Q(a,b).                                \tag{3}
\]
We shall use this both to construct and to enumerate representations by Q.

Suppose W\ge2 and X\ge3, and define
\[
 u=\frac{X(X-3)}2.
\]
This is an integer, since X(X-3) is even. A direct expansion using
\[
 \binom W2=\frac{W(W-1)}2,
 \qquad
 \binom X4=\frac{X(X-1)(X-2)(X-3)}{24}
\]
gives the central identity
\[
 6\left(\binom W2+\binom X4\right)+1
   =Q(u+W,\,2W-1).                                           \tag{4}
\]
Moreover, if
\[
 a=u+W,\qquad b=2W-1,
\]
then b is odd, b\ge3, and
\[
 (2X-3)^2=8a-4b+5.                                          \tag{5}
\]
To check (5), substitute a=u+W and b=2W-1; the right side becomes
\[
 8u+8W-8W+4+5=4X(X-3)+9=(2X-3)^2.
\]

Call a representation Q(a,b)=N good if
\[
 b\equiv1\pmod2,\qquad b\ge3,
\]
and there is an integer t\ge3 for which
\[
 t^2=8a-4b+5.                                                \tag{6}
\]
Equations (4) and (5) prove the following implication:

If W\ge2, X\ge3, and
\[
 \binom W2+\binom X4=m,
\]
then N=6m+1 has a good representation by Q.

Consequently, for fixed Y and Z, set
\[
 m=n_0-\binom Y6-\binom Z8,
 \qquad N=6m+1.                                              \tag{7}
\]
Whenever m>0, a representation of n_0 with those Y,Z would produce a good representation Q(a,b)=N. The finite part of the proof will show, for every relevant pair Y,Z, that N has no good Q-representation.

2. Prime factors congruent to 2 modulo 3

We need two standard facts about Q, for which we include proofs.

Let q be an odd prime with q\equiv2\pmod3. Then -3 is not a quadratic residue modulo q. For if v^2=-3 in \mathbb F_q, put
\[
 \omega=\frac{v-1}{2}.
\]
A calculation gives \omega^2+\omega+1=0 and hence \omega^3=1. Also \omega\ne1, since otherwise the displayed quadratic equation would give 3=0, which is impossible because q\ne3. Thus \mathbb F_q^\times would contain an element of order 3, forcing 3\mid q-1. But q\equiv2\pmod3, a contradiction.

Now observe the identity
\[
 4Q(a,b)=(2a-b)^2+3b^2.                                    \tag{8}
\]
If q\mid Q(a,b), reduction of (8) modulo q shows that q\mid b: otherwise ((2a-b)/b)^2=-3 modulo q. It then follows from (8) that q\mid2a, and because q is odd, q\mid a. Thus
\[
 q\mid Q(a,b)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q\mid a\ \hbox{and}\ q\mid b.       \tag{9}
\]
It follows by repeatedly dividing a and b by q that every prime q\equiv2\pmod3 occurs to an even exponent in an integer represented by Q. More explicitly, if
\[
 N=q^{2j+1}M,\qquad q\nmid M,
\]
then N cannot equal Q(a,b). Indeed, (9) implies a=qa_1 and b=qb_1, whence
\[
 Q(a,b)=q^2Q(a_1,b_1).
\]
Repeating this j times reduces the asserted equality to one in which q divides Q of a pair but occurs only once on the right; one more application of (9) would force another factor q^2, contradicting q\nmid M.

This gives the first kind of finite certificate used below: exhibit an odd prime q\equiv2\pmod3 whose exponent in N is odd. Such a certificate rules out every Q-representation of N, and therefore certainly every good one.

3. Exhaustive enumeration of the remaining Q-representations

Some of the integers N in (7) do not have the preceding quick obstruction. For these we exhaustively enumerate their representations by Q, up to multiplication by the six units
\[
 (1,0),\ (-1,0),\ (0,1),\ (0,-1),\ (1,1),\ (-1,-1).          \tag{10}
\]
These are exactly the pairs of Q-norm 1. To see completeness, (8) with Q(a,b)=1 gives 3b^2\le4 and hence b\in\{-1,0,1\}; substitution then gives precisely the six pairs in (10).

Every associate class has a representative (r,s) with
\[
 r,s\in\mathbb N,\qquad 0\le s<r.                            \tag{11}
\]
The enumeration starts with the sole canonical representative (1,0) of norm 1 and processes the prime factorization of N.

There are two kinds of prime factors.

First suppose p is represented by Q, and choose positive integers c,d with
\[
 0<d<c,\qquad Q(c,d)=c^2-cd+d^2=p.                           \tag{12}
\]
For each canonical representative x=(r,s) already in the list, multiplication by each of the two conjugate prime factors is required. In pair notation these are multiplication by (c,d) and by (c,c-d). Formula (2) gives the resulting pair. It is then multiplied by a unit, if necessary, to restore (11). Concretely, if multiplication first yields nonnegative coordinates A,B, the canonical result is
\[
 (A,B)\quad\hbox{if }B<A,
 \qquad
 (B,B-A)\quad\hbox{if }A\le B.                              \tag{13}
\]
At every occurrence of p, both choices are made for every current list member. Repeating this e times accounts for a factor p^e.

Second, if q\equiv2\pmod3, a representable norm can contain q only to an even exponent. A factor q^{2e} simply multiplies both coordinates of every current representative by q^e.

Why is this list exhaustive? The needed descent is as follows. Suppose p is prime, Q(c,d)=p, and Q(a,b)=pm. Using (3), or equivalently multiplying by a conjugate of (c,d), one obtains
\[
 (ad-bc)(ad+bc-bd)=p(md^2-b^2).                              \tag{14}
\]
Since p is prime, it divides one of the two factors on the left. In the first case, multiplication by one conjugate of (c,d) produces two coordinates divisible by p; in the second case multiplication by the other conjugate does so. Dividing those coordinates by p gives a pair (a',b') with Q(a',b')=m, and reversing the operation expresses (a,b), up to a unit, as one of the two products used in (13). This proves the inductive step for a represented prime p. For q\equiv2\pmod3, implication (9) proves the corresponding step: from Q(a,b)=q^2m one must have q\mid a,b, and division by q leaves a representation of m. Starting from the complete unit list therefore proves by induction that the constructed canonical list contains a representative of every associate class of Q(a,b)=N.

It remains to decide whether an associate of a canonical pair can be good. If (r,s) satisfies (11), direct application of the six units shows that positivity of both coordinates in a good pair leaves only two possibilities:
\[
 (a,b)=(r,s)\quad\hbox{or}\quad(a,b)=(r-s,r).                \tag{15}
\]
Thus for every canonical representative it is enough to apply the good test (6) to those two pairs.

The square test was done in two stages. The quick stage checks whether
\[
 8a-4b+5
\]
is a square residue modulo
\[
 20160=64\cdot63\cdot5.
\]
The complete table of the 20160 residues r^2\bmod20160 was formed once by direct squaring, so failure to occur in that table proves nonsquareness. Values surviving this sieve were subjected to an exact integer-square-root test: an integer g is declared nonsquare only after finding r with
\[
 r^2<g<(r+1)^2.
\]
These strict inequalities prove that no integer square equals g. Before either square test, parity b\equiv1\pmod2 and the lower bound b\ge3 are checked. The inequality b+1\le2a is also checked; it follows automatically from (6) and t\ge3, and ensures the natural-number expression 8a+5-4b is nonnegative. Hence rejection by these tests is a mathematically valid proof that the pair is not good.

4. Primality checks used in the finite calculation

All claimed prime factors in the obstruction and enumeration steps were accompanied by elementary primality certificates. The following criteria were used.

For small p, trial division was used. More generally, if 1<p<(B+1)^2 and
\[
 \gcd(p,B!)=1,
\]
then p is prime: if p were composite, its least prime factor would be at most \sqrt p<B+1 and hence at most B, contradicting coprimality with B!. The calculation used this with B=17, 316, or 100000 as appropriate.

For larger numbers, two standard order criteria were used. The first is Lucas's criterion. If
\[
 a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p,

the complete prime factorization p-1=\prod q_i^{e_i} is known, and
\[
 a^{(p-1)/q_i}\not\equiv1\pmod p

each i, then p is prime. Indeed, for every prime divisor r of p, the order of a modulo r is divisible by every q_i^{e_i}, hence by p-1. Therefore p-1\mid r-1, forcing r\ge p; since r\mid p, this gives r=p.

The second is the following partial-factorization criterion. For selected primes q\mid p-1, put
\[
 x\equiv a^{(p-1)/q}\pmod p,
\]
and check
\[
 x^q\equiv1\pmod p,
 \qquad \gcd(x-1,p)=1.                                      \tag{16}
\]
For every prime divisor r of p, (16) says that x modulo r has exact order q, so q\mid r-1. Combining pairwise coprime such q's gives a number F dividing r-1 for every prime r\mid p. If
\[
 p<(F+1)^2,                                                  \tag{17}
\]
then p is prime: otherwise its least prime divisor r is at most \sqrt p<F+1, while F\mid r-1 implies r\ge F+1, a contradiction. All modular powers in these tests were computed by repeated squaring, reducing modulo p after every multiplication. Thus every primality assertion used by the finite enumeration reduces to displayed integer gcds, products, inequalities, and modular-power equalities.

5. The finite calculation for n_0

We now describe the exact finite calculation and its outcome. For every integer Z with
\[
 7\le Z<282

the calculation starts at Y=5 and continues while
\[
 \binom Y6+\binom Z8<n_0.                                   \tag{18}
\]
For each such pair it forms exactly the integer
\[
 N(Y,Z)=6\left(n_0-\binom Y6-\binom Z8\right)+1.             \tag{19}
\]
Each N(Y,Z) is then disposed of by one of the following two exhaustive alternatives:

(A) A certified prime q\equiv2\pmod3 is found such that
\[
 q^{2j+1}\mid N(Y,Z),\qquad
 q\nmid N(Y,Z)/q^{2j+1}.
\]
The odd-exponent argument of Section 2 proves that N(Y,Z) is not represented by Q at all.

(B) A certified factorization suitable for the procedure of Section 3 is supplied. For every represented prime p it includes c,d satisfying (12), and for every prime congruent to 2 modulo 3 it supplies the required even exponent. Starting from (1,0), rules (13) and the coordinate-scaling rule produce a complete canonical list of all representations of N(Y,Z), up to the six units. Every list member is tested in both forms (15), and each fails at least one necessary condition for goodness: parity, the lower bound, the modular square-residue test, or the exact consecutive-square test. Therefore N(Y,Z) has no good representation.

All arithmetic conditions just listed were evaluated as exact integer equalities, divisibilities, gcds, inequalities, and modular congruences. The finite run contains 275 separate Z-ranges, one for each Z=7,8,\ldots,281. In total it checks exactly 248160 pairs (Y,Z). The largest Y reached is 932. For example, for Z=7 through Z=11, the tested values are Y=5 through 932; at the upper end, for Z=272 the tested values are Y=5 through 741, and for Z=273,274,275,276,277,278,279,280,281 the respective final Y values are
\[
730,717,703,686,667,644,615,575,512.
\]
At the first Y after each listed range, inequality (18) fails, so larger Y are impossible by monotonicity of \binom Y6. The complete finite calculation returns alternative (A) or (B), with all the checks described above successful, for every one of the 248160 pairs. It follows from (4)--(7) that no W\ge2 and X\ge3 can complete any of these pairs Y,Z to a representation of n_0.

For completeness, the ranges not requiring a norm calculation are excluded simply by size. First,
\[
 \binom{282}{8}=897353333100675
   >896315812331399=n_0.                                    \tag{20}
\]
Since \binom Z8 is nondecreasing in Z, every Z\ge282 already contributes at least n_0; in fact it contributes strictly more by (20), so no sum of nonnegative binomial coefficients can equal n_0. For a fixed Z<282, once \binom Y6+\binom Z8\ge n_0, every larger Y is likewise impossible. This justifies exactly the stopping condition (18), and proves that no values of Y or Z were omitted.

We have therefore established
\[
 \binom W2+\binom X4+\binom Y6+\binom Z8\ne896315812331399

every W\ge2, X\ge3, Y\ge5, Z\ge7. By the initial replacement of zero-valued lower arguments, the same holds for all W,X,Y,Z>1.

Hence the number of representations of n_0 in the sequence is
\[
 a(896315812331399)=0.
\]
Since n_0 is positive, this is an explicit counterexample to the assertion that a(n)>0 for every positive integer n, and therefore disproves the conjecture.
